tagline: Road and railroad trade levels through the Feather River Canyon.
intro: Highway 70 drops from Jarbo Gap into the North Fork Feather River canyon, following the river past bridges and three tunnels cut through rock. The Feather River Scenic Byway is a National Forest Scenic Byway paralleling the former Western Pacific Railroad’s Feather River Route.

The highway began with a railroad construction road. After Western Pacific completed its main line in 1909, residents formed the Plumas County Road Association in 1911 to campaign for a year-round Oroville-to-Quincy route. The existing ridge road closed for at least four months each winter. Before construction, the choice of route was contested: the state announced plans to improve the ridge road in 1916, but a 1919 bond amendment specified the Feather River alignment. Construction began in 1928, using incarcerated workers on easier sections and contractors elsewhere; the highway was dedicated in 1937 after Depression-era delays.

From SR 149, drive northeast out of the Sacramento Valley and cross the double-decker West Branch Bridge, with the railway below. Beyond Jarbo Gap come Pulga, the tunnels and the canyon toward Paxton. Turn southeast with SR 89 toward Quincy in the American Valley, then continue through Blairsden and Portola to Beckwourth. Highway 70 crosses the broad Sierra Valley and Beckwourth Pass before ending at US 395 at Hallelujah Junction.

moments.title: Pulga Bridge
moments.text: At Pulga, the highway passes above the railroad as both cross the North Fork Feather River. The upper crossing is an arch; the lower one is a railroad truss. Beyond it, three highway tunnels penetrate the canyon’s rock formations. Those tunnels were built at Arch Rock, Grizzly Dome and Elephant Butte during the highway project. At Arch Rock and Grizzly Dome, surveyors worked suspended on ropes over steep granite slopes, while rockslides repeatedly delayed construction. The California Highway Commission dedicated the completed road at Grizzly Dome on August 14, 1937, halfway between the ends of the project.
moments.notice: The highway arch crosses above the lower railroad truss bridge.

moments.title: Tobin Bridges
moments.text: Tobin reverses the arrangement at Pulga: here the railroad crosses above Highway 70. Both bridges span the North Fork Feather River, their paths nearly crossing on its western side. The rail bridge belongs to Union Pacific’s Feather River Route, originally built for Western Pacific. It forms part of the eastward climb toward Beckwourth Pass, maintaining the railroad’s overall compensated grade of one percent. The railway connects the Sacramento Valley with Salt Lake City through the Feather River valley. Elsewhere in the canyon, road and railway usually occupy opposite sides of the river.
moments.notice: At this crossing, the railroad passes above the highway.

moments.title: Paxton
moments.text: Two creeks join just upstream of Paxton to make the East Branch North Fork Feather River. From their confluence, the river winds west through a steep, narrow canyon, with Highway 70 on the north bank and the railway on the south. Near Paxton, the highway joins SR 89 and turns southeast, partly following Spanish Creek toward Quincy. Paxton was once called Soda Bar; its post office operated from 1917 to 1952. The creeks lead into different valleys: Indian Creek runs through Indian Valley, while Spanish Creek passes through the American Valley, home to Quincy.
